excerpts.text: A recent and controversial theory attributes the onset of the Younger Dryas (YD) climate interval, extinction of large mammalian fauna across North America, demise of the North American Clovis culture, and a range of other effects ~12,900 years ago to an extraterrestrial impact event (Firestone et al., 2007a, Kennett et al., 2009a, Kennett et al., 2009b).

Post-glacial warming during the Bølling–Allerød period reversed starting about 12,900 cal BP (calibrated years before present), with colder conditions prevailing during the ~1300-year Younger Dryas (YD) interval (Broecker et al., 2010, Meltzer and Holliday, 2010). In North America, an estimated 33 genera of mammalian megafauna (fauna >100 kg; e.g., mammoths, mastodons, giant short-faced bear, saber-tooth tigers; Barnosky et al., 2004) went extinct at about this time, followed shortly thereafter by extinction of ~50 mammalian genera in South America (Barnosky et al., 2004, Fiedel, 2009).
The beginning of the YD coincides approximately with the end of the Paleoindian Clovis-type lithic technology (Haynes, 2010, Meltzer and Holliday, 2010).

These early sources contain a number of suggestions – impact origin of glacial drumlins, supernova eruptions leading to “deadly nerve toxins” in Pleistocene algal mats, etc. – that are highly unlikely.

excerpts.text: The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis suggests that multiple extraterrestrial airbursts or impacts resulted in the Younger Dryas cooling, extensive wildfires, megafaunal extinctions and changes in human population.

We show that there are three challenges related to the timing of the event: accurate age control for some of the sites that are reported to provide evidence for the impact, linking these sites to the onset of the Younger Dryas and, most importantly, an apparent age discrepancy of up to two centuries between different sites associated with the proposed impact event. We would like to stress that if the markers at different locations have been deposited at different points in time, they cannot be related to the same event.

excerpts.text: Lawrence Edwardsj,k aInstitute of Global Environmental Change, Xi’an Jiaotong University, 710054 Xi’an, China; bState Key Laboratory of Loess and Quaternary Geology, Institute of Earth Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, 710061 Xi’an, China; cKey Laboratory of Karst Dynamics, Ministry of Land and Resources, Institute of Karst Geology, Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, 541004 Guilin, China; dInstitute of Geology, University of Innsbruck, 6020 Innsbruck, Austria; eDepartment of Earth Sciences, California State University, Dominguez Hills, Carson, CA 90747; fDepartamento de Geología, Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales, Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas, 28034 Madrid, Spain; gInstituto Pirenaico de Ecología, Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas, 50059 Zaragoza, Spain; hInstituto de Geociências, Universidade de São Paulo, 05508-090 São Paulo, Brazil; iScripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093; jDepartment of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN 55455; and kSchool of Geography, Nanjing Normal University, 210023 Nanjing, China Edited by Mark Thiemens, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, and approved August 5, 2020 (received for review April 23, 2020) The Younger Dryas (YD), arguably the most widely studied millennial-scale extreme climate event, was characterized by diverse hydrocli-mate shifts globally and severe cooling at high northern latitudes that abruptly punctuated the warming trend from the last glacial to the present interglacial.

Our analysis suggests that the onsets of YD in the North Atlantic (12,870 ± 30 B.P.) and the Asian Monsoon-Westerlies region are essentially synchronous within a few decades and lead the onset in Antarctica, implying a north-to-south climate signal propagation via both atmospheric (decadal-time scale) and oce-anic (centennial-time scale) processes, similar to the Dansgaard– Oeschger events during the last glacial period.

Within this framework at subcentennial precision, we further discuss the hypothesis of an extraterrestrial-impact trigger for the YD (13). Our results shed light on the underly-ing dynamics of the YD, particularly with respect to its trigger, transition, and termination.

excerpts.text: The **Younger Dryas impact hypothesis** (YDIH) is a [fringe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fringe_theory "Fringe theory")[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) hypothesis that posits that the cause of the disruption of the [Atlantic meridional overturning circulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_meridional_overturning_circulation "Atlantic meridional overturning circulation") resulting in the onset of the [Younger Dryas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Younger_Dryas "Younger Dryas") cooling c. 12,900 years [Before Present](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Present "Before Present"), was the result of an [impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_event "Impact event") or [air burst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteor_air_burst "Meteor air burst") of a [meteor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteor "Meteor"), possibly a [comet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet "Comet").

The YDIH was formally introduced in 2007 by nuclear physicist Richard Firestone and collaborators in the *[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proceedings_of_the_National_Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_United_States_of_America "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America")*[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) with the paper titled "Evidence for an extraterrestrial impact 12,900 years ago that contributed to the megafaunal extinctions and the Younger Dryas cooling." Prior to that publishing, in 2001, Firestone and archaeologist William Topping published their first version of YDIH, "Terrestrial Evidence of a Nuclear Catastrophe in [Paleo-Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleo-Indians "Paleo-Indians") Times" in *Mammoth Trumpet*, a newsletter of the Center for the Study of the First Americans.[[5]](#cite_note-Pinter_et_al_2011-5)

Firestone and collaborators elaborated on the hypothesis substantially in their 2006 book *The Cycle of Cosmic Catastrophes*, though one of its co-authors denies the book was meant to be scientific.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Pinter_et_al_2011-5) In the book, they argue that the impact broke an ice dam holding a massive reservoir of glacial meltwater, [Lake Agassiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Agassiz "Lake Agassiz"), causing it to flood the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") with freshwater disrupting the [North Atlantic Conveyor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shutdown_of_thermohaline_circulation "Shutdown of thermohaline circulation"), and causing a sudden cooling event.[[1]](#cite_note-:2-1) They argue that the impact in the [Great Lakes region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_region "Great Lakes region") destabilized the [Laurentide ice sheet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentide_ice_sheet "Laurentide ice sheet") and took with it typical evidence of an impact which caused hemisphere-spanning wildfires and the North American [megafauna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megafauna "Megafauna") and a Paleo-Indian extinction event,[[5]](#cite_note-Pinter_et_al_2011-5) in particular the disappearance of the [Clovis culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_culture "Clovis culture").[[6]](#cite_note-:9-6) However, [genetic evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_evidence "Genetic evidence") indicates that the Clovis people migrated southward and adapted to the changes in their environment.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) Anthropologist [Vance T.

excerpts.text: The **Younger Dryas** (YD, Greenland Stadial GS-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) was the final climatic phase of the [Last Glacial Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period") that occurred from around 12,900 to 11,700 years [Before Present](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Present "Before Present") (c. 10,900 – c. 9,700 BC).[[3]](#cite_note-3) It is primarily known for the sudden or abrupt cooling in the Northern Hemisphere, when the North [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") cooled and annual air temperatures decreased by around 3 °C (5 °F) over [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), 2–6 °C (4–11 °F) in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and up to 10 °C (18 °F) in [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), in a few decades.[[4]](#cite_note-Carlson2013-4) Cooling in Greenland was particularly rapid, taking place over just 3 years or less.[[1]](#cite_note-Partin2015-1)[[5]](#cite_note-5) At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere experienced warming.[[4]](#cite_note-Carlson2013-4)[[6]](#cite_note-6) This period ended as rapidly as it began, with dramatic warming over around 50 years, the transition from the glacial [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene") epoch into the current [Holocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene "Holocene") interglacial.[[1]](#cite_note-Partin2015-1)
